The therapeutic landscape for breast cancer patients is rapidly evolving with novel therapies regularly receiving regulatory approval. Yet directing these treatments to patients likely to benefit while sparing those unlikely to respond from their toxicities remains a major challenge. Many modern therapies, like immunotherapy and ADCs, rely on tissue architecture to be effective. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a formidable clinical challenge. A major recent advance has been the development of KRAS inhibitors, which have shown considerable promise in clinical trials (1). For decades, KRAS was considered undruggable; however, these new inhibitors represent a potential turning point for patients with PDAC. Despite this progress, rapid therapy resistance has already been observed in both patients and pre-clinical mouse models, highlighting the urgent need to define the mechanisms that drive resistance and to identify rational combination therapies.
In our laboratory, we have established and validated a panel of genetically heterogeneous PDAC models. This PhD project will therefore identify malignant cell-intrinsic and malignant cell-extrinsic mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibition, including fibroblast-mediated mechanisms, across genetically distinct PDACs. title: Research Associate (Laurenti Lab) (Fixed Term)
description:
Applications are invited for a research associate to join Prof Laurenti's research group. The team combine state-of-the-art experimental and computational methods to study the unique biological and molecular properties of human Haematopoietic Stem Cells (HSCs) across the lifespan. A specific area of interest aims to investigate how somatic mutations acquired by HSC in the first decades of life alter HSC function and predispose to blood cancers and other age-related diseases.
The post holder will lead a project centred on how mutations in the coding and non-coding areas of transcription factors confer HSCs with a selective advantage and predispose to leukaemia. The scope of the project is to identify cellular and molecular mechanisms and novel therapeutic vulnerabilities for early intervention or even prevention of blood cancers.
The successful candidate is expected to lead on the project and conduct experiments independently. They will contribute to the larger team and will assist other lab members on communal task as/when required. They will also effectively communicate their work in writing and oral presentations at internal meetings and conferences. They may also assist in the supervision of master-level students undertaking research projects in the team.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a formidable clinical challenge. A major recent advance has been the development of KRAS inhibitors, which have shown considerable promise in clinical trials (1). For decades, KRAS was considered undruggable; however, these new inhibitors represent a potential turning point for patients with PDAC. Despite this progress, rapid therapy resistance has already been observed in both patients and pre-clinical mouse models, highlighting the urgent need to define the mechanisms that drive resistance and to identify rational combination therapies.
In our laboratory, we have established and validated a panel of genetically heterogeneous PDAC models. These studies have shown that malignant-cell genetics shape distinct, therapeutically actionable vulnerabilities through both cell-intrinsic programmes and changes in the surrounding tumour microenvironment [(2) and unpublished]. This PhD project will therefore identify malignant cell-intrinsic and malignant cell-extrinsic mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibition, including fibroblast-mediated mechanisms, across genetically distinct PDACs. description:
A Research Associate post is available in the Marine Ecology and Conservation Group, led by Dr Catharine Horswill, in the Department of Zoology at the University of Cambridge. Catharine is a quantitative marine ecologist with expertise in population modelling, demography and the application of ecological evidence to conservation and management.
Reliable stock assessments are essential for the sustainable management of tropical tuna fisheries worldwide. In representing complex population and fishery dynamics, assessment models rely on simplifying assumptions about biological processes, spatial structure and fisheries data. Understanding how these assumptions affect model performance and management advice is critical for identifying key sources of uncertainty and determining where methodological advances or improvements in fisheries data could most effectively strengthen future assessments.
The project will develop and apply high-resolution, simulation-based approaches to evaluate how assumptions about population biology and fisheries data influence stock assessment performance and management advice. The project will initially focus on Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna, with subsequent application to bigeye and skipjack tuna where appropriate.
Initial work will build on an existing high-resolution, spatially explicit simulation framework developed using the Spatial Population Model (SPM). SPM will be used to generate population and fishery scenarios that incorporate key sources of structural uncertainty, including spatial variation in growth and fishery selectivity, alternative population structures, and differences in the weighting of fisheries data. title: Research Assistant/associate in development of 4D image processing methods (Fixed Term)

The post holder will be located in Central Cambridge, UK.
Computed tomography (CT) has transformed fields by enabling non-destructive three-dimensional (3D) imaging. However, conventional CT is fundamentally limited by acquisition speed: high-quality 3D reconstruction typically requires thousands of X-ray radiographs acquired over a full specimen rotation, taking minutes to hours. This makes CT unsuitable for fast, transient phenomena such as additive manufacturing, impact, fracture and high-rate deformation.
We are launching an ambitious research programme to overcome this limitation and establish new approaches for X-ray tomography of rapidly evolving processes. Combining advances in X-ray hardware, computational imaging, machine learning and mechanics, the project aims to reconstruct the three-dimensional evolution of materials during dynamic deformation, moving beyond static CT towards true four-dimensional imaging in space and time.

A central challenge will be to combine X-ray measurements with physical knowledge of deformation processes. The project therefore offers significant scope to develop new physics-informed and data-driven approaches coupling computational imaging with models of material deformation, with considerable freedom to shape the computational research programme.

title: Senior Scientific Associate (Fixed Term)
description:
Join the Crossley Research Group at the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute, where we investigate RNA-DNA hybrid molecules known as R-loops and their role in human disease. Our research focuses on understanding how R-loops contribute to genome instability and inflammation, and how these molecules and the cellular responses they trigger can be harnessed for cancer detection and treatment. To learn more about the group, visit:
https://www.cruk.cam.ac.uk/research-groups/crossley-group/
We are looking for an experienced, scientifically driven and collaborative researcher to join our growing team. This role combines hands-on experimental research with opportunities to contribute to scientific support activities and laboratory operations. You will work closely with colleagues to advance projects through to publication, help establish new research directions and methodologies, and, if desired, take the lead on your own projects. You will also partner with our Senior Scientific Associate, Dr Mawer, to support the day-to-day management and smooth running of the laboratory.
What You'll Be Doing
Working across a range of cutting-edge research projects, you will use techniques including:
Molecular biology, such as cloning, western blotting, human cell culture, CRISPR/Cas gene editing, lentiviral infection and qPCR.
RNA and nucleic acid biochemistry, including RNA/DNA and RNA-DNA hybrid isolation, immunoprecipitations and pull-down assays.
Immunofluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry.
Genomics approaches, including next-generation sequencing (NGS) library preparation and bioinformatics analysis.

We are particularly interested in candidates with strong molecular biology and biochemistry expertise, alongside experience in mammalian cell and/or tissue culture. You should have in-depth knowledge in at least one of the following areas:
Genome stability
RNA biology
Chromatin biology
Innate immunity

Royal Museums Greenwich is a collection of diverse historical sites. The sites are the National Maritime Museum, Cutty Sark, the Royal Observatory, and the Queen’s House. If you are passionate about the role Museums play in the learning journeys of children and young people, then this is the role for you. We are looking for a dynamic individual to work with schools and teachers to support and inspire collections-based learning at the National Maritime Museum and the Queen’s House. You will also nurture relationships with key internal and external stakeholders, ensuring that audience voice is embedded into everything we do.
